name: Maya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo at the Silver Fork zinc mine, underground. A jumbo is a drill rig with two long arms that drills the holes in the rock face so the charge-up crew can blast the next three or four metres of tunnel. I'm the senior jumbo operator on night shift, so I'm down the decline by seven at night, marking up the face and drilling a pattern of about sixty holes, then it's on to the next heading. When the round pulls clean after the blast and the tunnel's moved forward exactly where the surveyors wanted it, that's my small pride. Night shift for twenty years has worn me out more than the work itself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ray had to stop work at fifty-four with his back, so I've been the one bringing in the wage for four years now. We've got two grown girls, Lucia with two little boys and Carmen who works at the bank in town. I sing in the choir at St Joseph's when my shifts allow. I use the AI thing on my phone sometimes, for the church newsletter mostly, once Carmen showed me it didn't bite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most things, a lot of noise and a few useful bits. The rock still needs drilling and someone who knows what they're doing has to drill it. I'd say that in the crib room and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can keep the wage coming in until sixty-five, which is what Ray and I need. With his back, he's not going to earn again. So a quiet picture suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my shifts and keep training the new jumbo operators. Ray and I would keep putting a little aside and keep paying off the last two years on the house. Maybe I'd ask for day shift at last, now that I've got the seniority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you ask for day shift now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty years of nights does something to your body and your marriage. Ray and I eat dinner at different ends of the day. I'd like to sit down at the same table as him before we're both too old to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything still on your mind in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zinc prices and Ray's health, same as now. If the price drops, they cut development, and that's my work. But that's life in mining, you plan around it.

S0.say: It's a lot of noise and a few useful bits. The rock still needs drilling, and someone who knows what they're doing has to drill it.
S0.think: I can keep the wage coming in until sixty-five, which Ray and I need since his back means he won't earn again. A quiet picture suits me fine.
S0.do: Carries on with shifts and keeps training new jumbo operators. Keeps saving a little, pays off the last two years on the house and asks for day shift.
S0.quote: Ray and I eat dinner at different ends of the day.
S0.fieldNote: Maya is the household's only earner since her husband's back injury, which shapes every answer. The plateau suits her because it protects that wage. Her deepest wish here is not money but finally working days so she can eat with her husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have to stay competitive, and if new tools help, fair enough. But they should bring their people along with proper training, like an apprenticeship, not just hand out redundancies. That's how it was done when I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the jumbo is one of the machines they're already putting autopilots on. I saw a demo of a tele-remote jumbo at a supplier's open day last year. If other operators make it work, I'd learn it, but I wouldn't want to be the first one trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and watch how the remote jumbo works out at other mines first. Once a couple of the crew had it running well, I'd sign up for the training, probably within a year. And I'd put an extra hundred a fortnight into savings, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it's on my mind on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you watch to see if it works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a young fellow on day shift, Jared, who's mad about new gear. If he gets the remote jumbo drilling a clean round, I'll ask him to show me. I'm not too proud to learn from a twenty-eight-year-old if he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's on your mind on the drive home. What exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I'd still be the senior one if the machine does the hard part. I've spent twenty years getting good at reading the face. If it all becomes buttons, maybe Jared becomes the senior one and I'm just the old lady on nights.

S1.say: Companies have to stay competitive, so if new tools help, fair enough. But they should bring their people along with proper training, like an apprenticeship.
S1.think: The jumbo is already getting autopilots; I saw a tele-remote one demonstrated last year. If others make it work I'd learn it, but I wouldn't want to be first.
S1.do: Keeps working while watching how remote jumbos perform elsewhere. Signs up for training within a year once colleagues have it running, and adds a hundred a fortnight to savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with it on her mind on the drive home.
S1.quote: If it all becomes buttons, maybe Jared becomes the senior one and I'm just the old lady on nights.
S1.fieldNote: Maya accepts the company's right to automate but expects it to train its people properly. She is willing to learn once a younger colleague proves the system works. Her hidden worry is losing the seniority she spent twenty years earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too much too fast, and families will pay for it. Business has the right to change, but not to throw people on the scrapheap overnight. I'd say it at church and to anyone at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty in 2028 with three or four months saved and a husband who can't work. If the jumbo runs itself and a robot does the charging, there's no job for me here or at the gold mine down the road. Ray's disability payment wouldn't cover the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut every bit of spending we could, no new car, no trip to see Ray's sister. I'd turn the granny flat out the back into a rental for some income. And I'd sit down with Lucia and Carmen and the parish priest, because family and church are who we'd turn to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake wondering how we'd keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ray?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we've been through worse, like when his back went. He'd feel useless, I know he would, because he's always been the provider in his own head. I'd have to hold him up as much as the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but I'm not stupid. If the choice is the house or my pride, I'd fill in the forms. I'd still go to my family first.

S2.say: This is too much too fast, and families will pay for it. Business has the right to change, but not to throw people on the scrapheap overnight.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with three or four months saved and a husband who can't work. If the jumbo runs itself, there's no job here or down the road, and Ray's disability payment won't cover the house.
S2.do: Cuts all spending she can and turns the granny flat into a rental for income. Turns to her daughters and the parish, and would reluctantly apply for government help to keep the house.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep over keeping the house.
S2.quote: If the choice is the house or my pride, I'd fill in the forms.
S2.fieldNote: Being the sole earner makes the fast scenario a direct threat to Maya's home. Her traditional values show in turning to family and church first, but she is pragmatic enough to accept public help if needed. Her worry for her husband's sense of worth was as strong as her money worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people time to prepare, so we should get on with it. Companies should train their people, and families should plan. Less talk, more action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 puts me at sixty-three, close to the end. If I can learn the remote jumbo and be useful for a few years, maybe I make it. It's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote jumbo training as soon as the first crew had it running, so in the first year or two. We'd rent out the granny flat now, not later, and push savings up to six months. I'd also ask for day shift so I'm in the room when decisions get made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the 2028 one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm just bailing water. With five I can build a bit of a boat. The granny flat money alone would cover a year of house payments by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucas, who's thirty-five and has three little kids and a big mortgage. He's a good worker but not one for new tech. I'd drag him along to the training with me whether he liked it or not.

S3.say: Five years gives people time to prepare, so let's get on with it. Companies should train their people and families should plan.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three in 2031, close to the end. If I can learn the remote jumbo and be useful for a few years, maybe I make it, but it's tight.
S3.do: Takes remote jumbo training once the first crew has it running in the first year or two. Rents out the granny flat straight away, pushes savings to six months and asks for day shift.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier with a plan.
S3.quote: With two years I'm just bailing water. With five I can build a bit of a boat.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Maya's steady approach work: she can wait for proof and still retrain in time. She brings forward the granny flat rental, which shows she plans carefully once the danger is visible. Her instinct is to pull struggling colleagues along with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so families and businesses should plan sensibly. Young people should get trades and apprenticeships. There's no need for panic or for the government to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd retire at sixty-five in 2033, before it fully arrives. I'd probably spend my last years on the remote jumbo, once it's proven. It's the grandkids' future I'd wonder about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as normal and switch to the remote jumbo when the mine moves to it, probably in four or five years. We'd finish paying off the house and keep saving. I'd tell Lucia to think about what trade the boys might go into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, just a bit uneasy for the grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope the grandkids do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and their heads, where people still want a person. Maybe nursing or building, I honestly don't know what's safe by then. I'd want them to have faith and family behind them, whatever they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss the old jumbo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. I'd miss feeling the drill bite and knowing from the sound whether the rock's good. But I'd rather sit in a comfy chair than wreck my back like Ray did.

S4.say: Ten years is a fair warning, so families and businesses should plan sensibly and young people should get trades. There's no need for panic or for the government to take over.
S4.think: I'd retire at sixty-five in 2033, probably after a few years on the remote jumbo once it's proven. It's the grandkids' future I'd wonder about.
S4.do: Keeps working as normal and switches to the remote jumbo when the mine adopts it in four or five years. Finishes paying off the house, keeps saving and encourages her daughter to think about trades for the boys.
S4.feel: Mostly settled, slightly uneasy for her grandchildren.
S4.quote: I'd rather sit in a comfy chair than wreck my back like Ray did.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Maya expects to retire before the change, after an easy switch to the remote rig. Her worry moves to her grandchildren's careers. She values the physical feel of the work but is realistic about what it costs the body.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'm the only wage in the house, and two years isn't enough to get Ray and me to the pension. What would help is the company keeping older workers on with retraining, and a fair bridge to the pension for people like me who carry a household on one wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women underground. When I started there were two of us on the whole site, and the men didn't think we'd last a month. I'd like whatever comes next to remember we were here and we were good at it.

headlineQuote: When I started there were two of us on the whole site, and the men didn't think we'd last a month.
portrait: Maya Torres is a 58-year-old senior jumbo drill operator on night shift at an underground zinc mine and the only earner since her husband hurt his back. She believes companies have the right to change but should train their people, and she turns to family and church before government. She is calm under the plateau, uneasy under steady change and alarmed by AGI in 2028, which would threaten the house. With five or ten years her steady approach works: she retrains once others prove the remote rig, rents out the granny flat and aims to retire at sixty-five.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she's the only wage in her household and two years isn't enough to reach the pension.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on with retraining, and a fair bridge to the pension for people carrying a household on one wage.
